stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Collagraphy is a printmaking method in which textured materials are glued onto a board, inked, and pressed onto paper. It has often been treated as a classroom exercise rather than a serious medium. Yet Brazilian artist Tereza Moraes has built a three-decade career around it. Moraes layers fishing net, sand, and torn cardboard onto her plates, producing prints whose ridges can be felt as well as seen. Because the fragile surfaces wear down after five or six impressions, her editions are unusually small, and collectors now seek them out.
choices: To explain why Moraes's collagraph plates wear down after only five or six impressions
To introduce an artist who has built a serious career on a method often seen as elementary
To argue that art schools should teach collagraphy instead of more traditional printmaking methods
To contrast the materials Moraes uses with those favored by earlier collagraph artists
explanation: Every sentence serves one profile. The text defines collagraphy, notes that people often treat it as a classroom exercise, and then turns with 'Yet' to Moraes, whose long career, distinctive plates, and sought-after editions show the method used seriously. Choice B covers that whole arc, and 'introduce' matches the text's neutral, informative tone.

A.why: You picked a true detail. The plates do wear down quickly, but that is one supporting fact in a text about Moraes and her career, not the purpose of the whole passage.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text never recommends anything to art schools. It describes an artist and does not argue for a change in curriculum.

D.why: You brought in a comparison the text doesn't make. No earlier collagraph artists are mentioned, so the text cannot be contrasting Moraes's materials with theirs.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Hydrologists call a river a "losing stream" when it feeds water into the ground beneath it instead of drawing water from it. Streams are not fixed in one category, though: a stream can shift between gaining and losing as the water table around it rises and falls. The Arroyo Pinto in northern Mexico is a case in point. During the summer rains, groundwater near its channel sits high enough to seep into the stream. By late winter, the surrounding aquifer has dropped so far that the arroyo's water drains downward, and the channel runs dry within a few kilometers.
choices: To explain a hydrological category and show how a single stream can move in and out of it
To describe the summer rains that raise groundwater levels near the Arroyo Pinto each year
To argue that losing streams are more vulnerable to drought than hydrologists have assumed
To show that the Arroyo Pinto remains a losing stream during every season of the year
explanation: The text defines a 'losing stream,' states the general rule that streams can switch between gaining and losing, and then uses the Arroyo Pinto to illustrate that rule. Choice A covers the definition, the rule, and the example together.

B.why: You chose one real detail. The summer rains appear only as part of the example, and the text is about the stream's changing relationship to groundwater, not about the rains.

C.why: You read in an argument the text never makes. It says nothing about drought vulnerability or about what hydrologists have wrongly assumed. It only explains and illustrates.

D.why: You reversed the example. In summer, groundwater seeps into the Arroyo Pinto, so it is gaining then. It becomes a losing stream only in late winter.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, the fossil plant Velatophyllum, known only from scattered leaf impressions in Antarctic rock, was assumed to be a fern. However, specimens recovered in 2019 preserve small seeds attached to the leaf bases, and ferns reproduce by spores, not seeds. Those seeds have thick protective coats, and the plant's leaves grew in tight, leathery clusters. Together, these features have led paleobotanists to reclassify Velatophyllum as an early seed plant, one apparently suited to surviving long, dark polar winters.
choices: To explain why ferns reproduce by spores rather than by producing seeds on their leaves
To argue that most plant fossils found in Antarctica have been misidentified by researchers
To describe how new specimens changed scientists' view of what kind of plant a fossil was
To show that the 2019 specimens confirmed that Velatophyllum was an unusual kind of fern
explanation: The text opens with a long-held assumption that Velatophyllum was a fern, turns on 'However' to the 2019 seed-bearing specimens, and ends with the plant's reclassification. Choice C covers that old-view-to-new-view structure for the fossil as a whole.

A.why: You picked a supporting fact. The point about spores is there only to show why seeds rule out a fern. It is a step in the reasoning, not the text's purpose.

B.why: You generalized beyond the text. It discusses one misidentified fossil and says nothing about most Antarctic plant fossils, and it doesn't argue a broad claim.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. The 2019 specimens overturned the fern classification rather than confirming it, and Velatophyllum was reclassified as a seed plant.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Metallic glasses are alloys cooled so quickly that their atoms freeze in a disordered arrangement instead of forming crystals, which makes them unusually strong and springy. For decades, however, they could be produced only as thin ribbons or small pieces, because thicker samples cooled too slowly at their centers and crystallized. Engineer Hana Okafor's team has now developed an iron-based alloy that stays glassy at thicknesses of several centimeters. Its first commercial use, in springs for precision watches, exploits the material's ability to flex millions of times without permanently deforming.
choices: To explain why rapid cooling keeps the atoms in certain alloys from arranging into crystals
To argue that metallic glasses will soon replace steel in most kinds of industrial manufacturing
To show that metallic glasses are weaker than ordinary metals but far more flexible than them
To describe a class of materials, a long-standing obstacle to making them, and a recent advance
explanation: The text moves in three steps. It says what metallic glasses are, then explains why they long couldn't be made thick ('however'), then presents Okafor's alloy and its first use. Choice D names those three parts in the order the text gives them.

A.why: You chose a true detail from the opening sentence. Rapid cooling is part of the definition, but the text goes on to cover a manufacturing limit and a breakthrough, which this choice leaves out.

B.why: You chose a verb and a claim that are too strong. The text mentions a single use in watch springs and makes no prediction about replacing steel.

C.why: You misread the properties. The text calls metallic glasses 'unusually strong,' not weaker than ordinary metals.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: City planners usually treat alleys as service corridors, places for trash bins and delivery trucks rather than for people. Kellbrook's Green Alley Program, launched in 2012, takes a different view. The program replaces cracked asphalt with permeable pavers that let rainwater soak into the soil, adds lighting and planters, and invites residents on each block to vote on features such as benches or murals. More than ninety of the city's alleys have now been converted, and several host weekend markets.
choices: To explain how permeable pavers reduce the amount of rainwater that flows into city drains
To describe a city program that treats alleys as public spaces rather than as service routes
To argue that other cities should adopt Kellbrook's approach to redesigning their alleys
To show that Kellbrook's alleys are still used mainly for trash collection and deliveries
explanation: After a brief note on how alleys are usually treated, the rest of the text describes the Green Alley Program: what it changes, how residents take part, and what has come of it. Choice B covers the whole text, and 'describe' fits its informative tone.

A.why: You picked a single feature. Permeable pavers are one element of the program, and the text doesn't explain drainage in any detail. It is profiling the program as a whole.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text reports what Kellbrook has done but never recommends the program to other cities.

D.why: You reversed the text. It describes how the program moved alleys away from purely service use, noting that ninety have been converted and some now host markets.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Musicologists long regarded the Ferrand Songbook, a manuscript of forty-eight part-songs from the 1590s, as the careful work of a single copyist. Close study of its ink and handwriting, however, has revealed at least four different hands. Several songs also appear twice, the second version apparently corrected after being performed. Scholars now describe the songbook not as a finished anthology but as a working collection, added to and revised by a circle of musicians over perhaps two decades.
choices: To explain how the study of ink and handwriting helps scholars date musical manuscripts
To argue that the Ferrand Songbook is the most important surviving set of 1590s part-songs
To describe how scholars have come to see a manuscript as a shared and evolving collection
To show that the Ferrand Songbook's songs were copied once and never revised afterward
explanation: The text presents the old view of the songbook as one copyist's work, turns on 'however' to the evidence of several hands and revised songs, and ends with the new view of a collaborative working collection. Choice C covers that whole shift.

A.why: You focused on the method rather than the subject. The ink and handwriting study is mentioned only as the source of the new evidence, and the text never discusses dating manuscripts.

B.why: You chose a claim the text never makes. It doesn't rank the songbook against other collections or argue for its importance.

D.why: You reversed the evidence. The text says several songs appear in a second, corrected version and that the collection was revised over decades.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: In some languages, a speaker cannot simply report that something happened; the grammar itself requires the speaker to indicate how they know it. Linguists call this feature evidentiality. In Tamuri, a language spoken by about 12,000 people in the Andean highlands, one verb suffix marks events the speaker witnessed, another marks events learned from others, and a third marks conclusions drawn from clues, such as wet ground indicating rain. Leaving the suffix off is not an option: a Tamuri sentence without one is ungrammatical.
choices: To describe a grammatical feature and illustrate it with a language that requires its use
To explain how Tamuri speakers conclude from wet ground that rain must have fallen
To argue that languages with evidentiality let speakers communicate more accurately
To show that Tamuri speakers may decide for themselves whether to mark their sources
explanation: The text begins with a general statement that some grammars require speakers to mark how they know something, names that feature evidentiality, and then uses Tamuri's three suffixes as a concrete example. Choice A covers both the general feature and the illustration.

B.why: You picked the most vivid detail. The wet-ground example only illustrates one of Tamuri's three suffixes and is not what the text as a whole is about.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text explains the feature neutrally and never claims it makes communication more accurate.

D.why: You missed the final sentence. It says leaving the suffix off is 'not an option,' so marking the source is required, not optional.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Surviving weavers' pattern books usually preserve textile designs but reveal little about the people who made them. The notebooks of Scottish weaver Janet Rennick (1821–1894) are an exception. Alongside samples of her checked woolens, Rennick recorded the price of each batch of yarn, the names of the neighbors who spun it, and the days her loom stood idle when dye shipments ran late. Historians have used the notebooks to reconstruct how a rural weaving household earned and lost money as factory cloth flooded local markets.
choices: To describe the checked woolen patterns that Rennick wove for customers in her village
To argue that the spread of factory cloth drove rural weaving households into poverty
To show that Rennick's notebooks, like most pattern books, contain only design samples
To describe a weaver's records and explain why they are valuable to historians of work
explanation: The text contrasts typical pattern books with Rennick's notebooks, lists what she recorded beyond designs, and ends with how historians have used those records. Choice D covers both what the notebooks contain and why they matter.

A.why: You chose a detail that really is in the text but is too narrow. The woolen samples are mentioned in passing, and the text's interest is in the business records kept alongside them.

B.why: You went beyond the text. It says the notebooks show how one household earned and lost money, and it doesn't argue that factory cloth impoverished rural weavers in general.

C.why: You reversed the text's central contrast. The notebooks are called 'an exception' because they record far more than designs.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, earthquake monitoring in rural Peru depended on a handful of costly stations spaced hundreds of kilometers apart. Seismologist Rosa Quispe Mamani has spent fifteen years filling the gaps between them. Her project, Red Escolar, installs palm-sized motion sensors in village schools, where teachers keep the devices powered and students log the readings each week. The network now includes more than 300 sites, and its records helped researchers locate a fault segment near Ayacucho that the older stations had never detected. Quispe also trains teachers to explain local earthquake risk to families.
choices: To argue that national agencies should replace their costly stations with sensors placed in schools
To describe a seismologist's effort to widen earthquake monitoring by placing sensors in rural schools
To explain how researchers used school-based records to locate a previously undetected fault segment
To describe how village students designed low-cost sensors to fill the gaps in a national network
explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first sentence names a gap in monitoring. The rest present Quispe's project: how it works, how big it has grown, what it found, and the teacher training that goes with it. Each one adds to a profile of her effort to extend monitoring through rural schools. The text informs and never argues, so the neutral verb 'describe' fits, and choice B covers the whole passage.

A.why: You picked a verb that's too strong. The text reports what Red Escolar has done but never says the older stations should be replaced, or makes any recommendation at all. 'Argue' needs an opinion the passage doesn't state.

C.why: You took a true detail for the purpose. The fault segment near Ayacucho is one result mentioned in one sentence. It can't explain why the text also covers the gap in monitoring, how the sensors are maintained, or the teacher training.

D.why: You misread who does what. Quispe's project installs the sensors, and students only log the weekly readings. Nothing in the text says students designed the devices.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Since 2009, the volunteers of the Marsh Line Atlas have mapped a stretch of Louisiana coastline that loses land nearly every year. Working from kayaks with handheld GPS units, they trace shorelines, abandoned canals, and the foundations of old fishing camps, then publish each season's survey as a free printed sheet. A map can keep a record of a place after the place itself is gone. Several islands on the group's 2011 sheet are now open water, and former residents use that sheet to find family homesites that no current map shows.
choices: To explain how former residents find family homesites by consulting older printed coastal maps
To argue that government agencies should rely on volunteers to map rapidly changing coastlines
To describe a volunteer group that maps a shrinking coastline and the lasting record its maps provide
To describe how a volunteer group uses satellite images to predict where the coastline will erode next
explanation: The text introduces the Marsh Line Atlas, explains how its volunteers work, and then states a general idea: a map can preserve a place after the place is gone. The 2011 islands and the former residents are an example of that idea. So the passage is both a profile of the group and an account of why its maps matter. Choice C is the only option that covers both parts, and 'describe' matches the passage's neutral tone.

A.why: You chose the last detail in the passage and treated it as the purpose. Former residents finding homesites is the example of the broader point, not what the whole text is for. This choice leaves out the group, its methods, and its seasonal surveys.

B.why: You read an argument into a passage that only informs. The text never mentions government agencies and never recommends who should do the mapping, so 'argue' claims more than the text supports.

D.why: You got the group's methods wrong. The volunteers survey from kayaks with handheld GPS units and record what is there now. The text says nothing about satellite images or forecasting future erosion.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Economists use the term "job lock" for a worker's decision to stay in a job that he or she would otherwise leave because quitting would mean giving up a benefit tied to that employer. In the United States, employer-provided health insurance is the most widely studied case. Pensions that vest only after several years of service can have the same effect, as can paid leave that builds up with seniority. Any benefit that cannot follow a worker to a new job can hold that worker in place.
choices: To argue that employers should allow workers to carry their benefits to new jobs
To describe a pattern in worker behavior and identify several benefits that can cause it
To explain why health insurance is the benefit that economists have studied most often
To show that workers who have pensions change jobs more often than workers without them
explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first sentence defines job lock, a pattern in how workers behave. The middle sentences list benefits that produce it: health insurance, pensions, and paid leave. The last sentence states the general rule behind them all. Choice B covers the definition and the examples, and its verbs, 'describe' and 'identify,' fit a text that informs without taking a side.

A.why: You picked a verb that is too strong. The text explains how non-portable benefits keep workers in place, but it never recommends what employers should do. 'Argue' needs an opinion that the text doesn't state.

C.why: You picked a true detail instead of the purpose. The text does say health insurance is the most studied case, but it never explains why, and that one sentence leaves out the pensions, the paid leave, and the general rule.

D.why: You reversed what the text says. Pensions that vest late make workers less likely to leave, and the text never compares workers who have pensions with workers who don't.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For much of the twentieth century, seismologists assumed that a fault either stayed locked or ruptured suddenly in an earthquake. However, GPS stations installed in the Pacific Northwest during the 1990s recorded something in between: sections of a fault slipping gradually over days or weeks, releasing as much energy as a moderate earthquake without producing noticeable shaking. Such "slow slip events" have since been detected in Japan, Mexico, and New Zealand, where they often recur at fairly regular intervals.
choices: To argue that GPS stations are more useful than seismometers for studying faults
To explain why slow slip events tend to recur at fairly regular intervals
To describe a kind of fault movement and note where it has been observed
To suggest that slow slip events cause stronger shaking than earthquakes do
explanation: The text opens with an old belief that faults either stay locked or rupture suddenly. It then introduces a third kind of movement, slow slip, says what it is like, and lists the places it has been found. Choice C covers the whole text: it describes the phenomenon and notes where it has been observed. The neutral verb 'describe' matches a text that informs.

A.why: You read a comparison and an opinion into the text. GPS stations are only how the events were first recorded. The text never mentions seismometers or ranks one instrument above another.

B.why: You picked a true detail instead of the purpose. The last sentence says the events often recur regularly, but the text never explains why, and that detail can't account for the rest of the passage.

D.why: You reversed a key detail. The text says slow slip releases energy without producing noticeable shaking, so it can't be stronger shaking than an earthquake.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: In the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, a fallen tree may lie on the ground for centuries as it slowly decays. During that time it often serves as a "nurse log." Its moss-covered surface holds moisture, and its height lifts seedlings of western hemlock and Sitka spruce above the dense ferns of the forest floor. When the log finally rots away, the trees it supported may be left standing in a straight row, their roots arching over the space where it once lay.
choices: To argue that fallen trees should be left in place rather than cleared from forests
To show that ferns on the forest floor help young seedlings take root and grow
To account for the straight rows of trees that are sometimes found in rainforests
To describe how fallen trees in certain forests support the growth of new trees
explanation: Every sentence is about the fallen log and the trees that grow on it: how long it lasts, what makes it a good seedbed, and what it leaves behind. Choice D covers the whole sequence, and 'describe' fits a passage that gives facts without offering an opinion.

A.why: You picked a verb that is too strong. The text explains what nurse logs do, but it never says how forests should be managed. 'Argue' needs an explicit recommendation, and the passage doesn't contain one.

B.why: You got the ferns' role backward. The log helps seedlings by lifting them above the dense ferns, so the ferns are something the seedlings need to escape. They don't help the seedlings grow.

C.why: You picked a true detail instead of the purpose. The straight rows appear only in the last sentence, as one result of the process. They don't explain why the text describes the log's moisture, height, and slow decay.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, nutrition researchers who wanted to know how many calories people burned in everyday life relied largely on participants' own activity diaries, which were often inaccurate. The doubly labeled water method changed that. A participant drinks water containing harmless, rare forms of hydrogen and oxygen, and urine samples collected over the next one to two weeks show how quickly each leaves the body. Because oxygen also exits as exhaled carbon dioxide, the gap between the two rates lets researchers calculate energy use while participants follow ordinary routines.
choices: To introduce a technique for measuring the energy people use in daily life and explain how it works
To argue that activity diaries should no longer be used in any kind of nutrition research study
To describe how the body releases oxygen in the form of carbon dioxide during normal breathing
To explain why participants in nutrition studies have trouble recording their activities accurately
explanation: The first sentence names a problem, and the second says a method solved it. Every sentence after that explains how the method works. Choice A covers the whole text: it introduces the technique and explains its workings. The verbs 'introduce' and 'explain' also fit the text's neutral, informative tone.

B.why: You read a recommendation into the text. It says diaries were often inaccurate, but it never argues that they should be dropped from all research. 'Argue' needs an explicit opinion, and the text doesn't give one.

C.why: You picked one supporting detail. The fact that oxygen leaves the body as carbon dioxide is mentioned only to explain why the method works. It is not what the text is about.

D.why: You focused on the opening background. The text mentions that diaries were inaccurate but never explains why. That sentence only sets up the method that the rest of the text describes.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Immunological memory can outlast the threat that created it by a remarkable span. In 2008, researchers drew blood from a group of people in their nineties and older who had lived through the 1918 influenza pandemic as children. These survivors still carried antibodies that recognized the 1918 virus. From some of them, the team isolated immune cells that went on to produce those same antibodies in the laboratory, roughly ninety years after the original infection.
choices: To illustrate, through one study, how long the immune system can retain its memory of an infection
To argue that the 1918 influenza pandemic was far less severe than historians have long assumed
To describe the laboratory procedure that scientists use to isolate cells that produce antibodies
To explain why young children were especially vulnerable to infection during the 1918 pandemic
explanation: The first sentence states a general rule and gives no names or dates. Everything after it is one concrete case that shows the rule at work: a study that found antibodies about ninety years after infection. Choice A names that structure: a single study used to illustrate how long immune memory lasts.

B.why: You inferred a historical claim the text never makes. The text says nothing about how severe the pandemic was or what historians believe. It is about how long antibodies last.

C.why: You latched onto the step of isolating cells, which is one finding of the study. The text never describes how the procedure is done, and that step only supports the larger point about lasting memory.

D.why: You treated a background detail as the topic. The survivors were children in 1918, but the text never discusses whether children were more vulnerable or why.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Ornithologist Amara Okonkwo-Hale has spent two decades banding swifts in Kenya's Rift Valley. Rather than tracking a single colony, she follows two: one nesting on sandstone cliffs, the other under the eaves of village houses. Her records show that the village birds now return each spring about nine days earlier than the cliff birds, a gap that has widened steadily since she began. Okonkwo-Hale has also trained more than forty local students to band birds, and many of them now run surveys of their own.

To introduce an ornithologist and describe the long-term fieldwork she has carried out

explanation: Every sentence is about Okonkwo-Hale and her work: how long she has banded swifts, the two colonies she follows, what her records show, and the students she has trained. A.why: The text reports a nine-day gap between the two colonies but never says what causes it. You picked a purpose the passage doesn't carry out, because the gap is its most striking detail.

C.why: 'Argue' needs an opinion stated in the text, and the passage never says one colony deserves more protection. You took a neutral description of two groups and read a recommendation into it.

D.why: This detail is true, but it comes only from the last sentence. You chose one achievement instead of a purpose that covers the colonies and the records as well.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: A roller-crimper is a heavy drum ringed with blunt, chevron-shaped blades that a tractor pushes across a field of cover crop such as cereal rye. Instead of cutting the plants, the blades crimp their stems, which kills them and lays them flat in a thick mat. Farmers then plant cash crops directly through the mat, which smothers weeds and holds moisture in the soil. In one multiyear trial, fields managed this way needed about a third as much herbicide as conventionally tilled fields.
choices: To argue that farmers should stop using herbicides and buy roller-crimpers instead
To describe how a farm tool works and what it offers the farmers who use it
To explain why cutting a cover crop works better than crimping its stems
To point out that the blades on a roller-crimper are shaped like chevrons
explanation: The passage moves from what the roller-crimper is, to how it handles the cover crop, to how farmers plant through the mat, to the herbicide savings in a trial. Every sentence tells you either how the tool works or what it does for farmers. The text informs and doesn't urge, so 'describe' fits, and B covers both halves.

A.why: The trial fields used about a third as much herbicide, not none, and the text never tells farmers what to buy. You turned a reported gap between two kinds of field into a recommendation the passage doesn't make.

C.why: The text says the blades crimp the plants 'instead of cutting' them and presents crimping as the useful step. This choice reverses that.

D.why: The blade shape is mentioned in the first sentence, but it is a passing detail. You picked something true about the tool instead of the purpose of the whole text.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Engineers have long treated a crack in a transparent solid as permanent: once a pane splits, it must be replaced. Materials chemist Ines Varga's team, however, has produced a clear polymer glass that mends itself at room temperature. When two broken edges are held together for about an hour, chemical bonds re-form across the gap, and the joined sample regains most of its original strength. Because the process requires no heat or adhesive, the material could extend the life of screens and windows that would otherwise be thrown away.
choices: To describe a new material that challenges the belief that cracked transparent solids cannot be repaired
To explain how chemical bonds re-form when the broken edges of a polymer are held together
To argue that device makers should replace conventional screen glass with Varga's new polymer
To show that Varga's polymer must be heated before its broken pieces can be joined again
explanation: Ask what every sentence has in common. The first sentence gives the old belief that cracks are permanent. 'However' brings in Varga's polymer, and the remaining sentences describe how it mends and why that matters. The text informs rather than argues, so 'describe' is the right verb, and this choice covers both the old belief and the new material that challenges it.

B.why: You picked a true detail. The text does mention bonds re-forming across the gap, but that is a single step in the description. It doesn't explain the old belief or why the material matters, so it is too narrow to be the purpose of the whole text.

C.why: The verb is too strong. The text says the material 'could extend the life' of screens, which is a neutral possibility, but it never says anyone should switch to it. 'Argue' needs an explicit recommendation, and the text doesn't make one.

D.why: This reverses the text. The polymer mends at room temperature, and the process 'requires no heat or adhesive.'

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Along some faults, strain is released through slow-slip events: movements that unfold over weeks and produce no shaking people can feel. It has been unclear whether these quiet episodes relieve stress on a fault or simply shift it elsewhere. To find out, geophysicist Tomás Arriaga examined fifteen years of GPS and seismic records from one Pacific fault. He found that after each slow-slip event, small earthquakes clustered along the edges of the slipping patch, suggesting that slow slip loads neighboring sections of the fault rather than easing pressure overall.
choices: To note that slow-slip events unfold over weeks and cause no shaking that people can feel
To show that slow-slip events steadily relieve the stress on neighboring parts of a fault
To describe research addressing an open question about how slow-slip events affect fault stress
To argue that slow-slip events should be used to forecast when large earthquakes will occur
explanation: The text names a gap ('It has been unclear whether...'), then describes Arriaga's study and what it found. Every sentence serves that structure of question, investigation, and answer. The text reports research and doesn't take a position, so 'describe' fits, and this choice covers the whole text instead of one part of it.

A.why: This is true, but it only restates the background definition in the first sentence. It leaves out the open question and the study, which make up most of the text.

B.why: This reverses the finding. Arriaga's records suggest that slow slip 'loads neighboring sections of the fault rather than easing pressure.'

D.why: The text never discusses forecasting large earthquakes or recommends any use for slow-slip data. 'Argue' is too strong for a text that only reports what a study found.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: In the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, a fallen tree is not simply debris. As a toppled hemlock or spruce decays, its moss-covered trunk holds moisture and nutrients, becoming a raised seedbed above the crowded forest floor. Seedlings that sprout on these "nurse logs" often grow in a straight row, and centuries later their roots may still straddle the space where the log once lay. A dead organism, in other words, can go on shaping a living community long after it falls.
choices: To explain why hemlock and spruce trees topple more often than other rainforest species do
To describe how fallen trees in some rainforests continue to support new growth as they decay
To point out that seedlings growing on nurse logs often appear in a straight row
To argue that fallen trees should be cleared so that seedlings can reach the forest floor
explanation: Every sentence is about what a fallen tree does for new plants. The trunk holds moisture and nutrients, seedlings take root on it, and their roots keep its shape for centuries. The last sentence states this as a general rule: a dead organism can go on shaping a living community. The tone is neutral exposition, so 'describe' fits, and this choice covers the whole text.

A.why: Hemlock and spruce are named only as examples of fallen trees. The text never says how often they topple or compares them with other species, so this choice adds a claim the text doesn't support.

C.why: You picked a true detail. The straight row of seedlings is one piece of evidence for the main idea, but it is too narrow to be the purpose of the whole text.

D.why: This reverses the text. The passage says fallen logs help seedlings by giving them a raised seedbed. It never suggests that clearing logs would help.
